THE ATTACK FAILED, AND IT FAILED ON THE PAGE RATHER THAN ON MY MEMORY. I fetched Wikisource's transcription of the 1862 Macmillan Goblin Market and Other Poems and read the whole sonnet out. It is headed REMEMBER. with Sonnet. beneath the heading, it runs fourteen lines, and it ends: 'Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.' Capital B on Better, capital T on Than at the head of line 14, full stop after sad. The proposal matches character for character, keeps the two lines as two lines in the edition's lineation with the poem's own capitals at each line head, and is not a prose sentence broken up.

THE LOCATOR IS RIGHT BY COUNT, NOT BY ASSERTION. I counted the sonnet from the transcription: Remember me when I am gone away (1), Gone far away into the silent land (2), When you can no more hold me by the hand (3), Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay (4), Remember me when no more day by day (5), You tell me of our future that you planned (6), Only remember me; you understand (7), It will be late to counsel then or pray (8), Yet if you should forget me for a while (9), And afterwards remember, do not grieve (10), For if the darkness and corruption leave (11), A vestige of the thoughts that once I had (12), Better by far you should forget and smile (13), Than that you should remember and be sad (14). Lines 13 to 14 is correct, and they are the closing couplet and the two lines the poem is known by, so the fame test holds on the closing-line ground rather than on a reference-book ground.

WHAT I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) Translation drift, the usual killer on this track: there is none to have, the poem is English-original and there is no translator between the card and the page. (2) Volume and date. Remember was written in 1849 and a reader might expect that date, but the citation is to the printing whose wording is quoted, the Macmillan first edition of 1862, which is what rule 4 asks for; the poem is in that volume and Wikisource's text is established from the scan of it. (3) Misattribution and the Dante Gabriel confusion. This is Christina Rossetti's sonnet, not her brother's, and it is not one of the brief's roving orphan lines. (4) Speaker. A sonnet in the poet's own voice; there is no character and none is owed in the source. (5) Scope. 1862, poetry, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. (6) Publishability, which is the only place I thought this might genuinely break. The sonnet is spoken by someone anticipating her own death, and the octave has 'gone far away into the silent land'; line 11 even has 'the darkness and corruption'. But the two lines taken are the turn away from all of that, they contain nothing graphic, and they would need no warning standing alone on a card at six in the morning. The card prints the couplet, not the sonnet. (7) Gates. shipped.js on the exact line with 'Christina Rossetti': shipped [], near [], christina rossetti at 1 of 3 for the year, standing in month 4, so the cap is not reached; not banned, not on personsAtCap, and no second Rossetti appears anywhere in the month's verdicts, so she does not stand twice in August. Source line is 95 characters, leads with her name, gives work then locator then volume, carries no dash and no straight double quote. Tag Poetry is the form of the work.

THEME AND THE SIX A.M. TEST. August is impermanence and the blurb asks for elegy that helps. This is the gentlest thing in the poetry lane: the whole force of the couplet is permission to let go and be glad, which is the opposite of famous-and-bleak. It is the strongest of the four lines I was given, and the citation is the cleanest.
